oneLine: Open models now trail the best closed models by weeks. You can run strong weights yourself, which makes serving them a core skill for any team shipping AI products.
summary:
In late 2022 a few hundred people did this work, most of them inside a handful of labs, and everyone else expected to rent intelligence through an API for good. Open models changed the picture. Hugging Face now hosts millions of them, and the strongest trail the best closed models by weeks.

Once your team runs the weights, three things become engineering choices instead of a vendor's defaults: how fast responses arrive, how often the service stays up, and what each token costs. The Preface argues that an inference strategy now separates differentiated products from thin wrappers. It also argues that you can still get good at this fast, because the field is young and the problems run from kernels to clusters with few experts on any of them.

mechanism.title: Labs held the weights
mechanism.body: In 2022 only a few companies trained frontier models; everyone else called their APIs.

mechanism.title: Open models caught up
mechanism.body: Open releases from late 2024 matched closed models' capability within weeks or months.

mechanism.title: Weights mean control
mechanism.body: Running your own model turns latency, availability and cost into things you can engineer.

mechanism.title: Teams need serving skills
mechanism.body: To compete, your team needs people who can serve models at low latency and low cost.

callout.name: You are early
callout.body: Companies want far more inference engineers than exist. Most of the hard problems are still open, so a newcomer who does the work can reach the frontier fast.

figureRefs.lookFor: The steep climb in the count of public models over five years.
Open and closed models each crossing the same capability lines, a little apart in time.
Customisation adding capability while you keep control of latency, reliability and cost.

keyCards.label: Latency
keyCards.title: Tune for real time
keyCards.body: Shared APIs tune for throughput across all their customers. You can tune your own deployment for fast replies.

keyCards.label: Availability
keyCards.title: From two nines to four
keyCards.body: Dedicated deployments can reach 99.99% uptime, where shared APIs often sit near 99%.

keyCards.label: Cost
keyCards.title: Cheaper per token at volume
keyCards.body: At high volume an open model can cost a fraction of a closed API per token.

workedExample.title: What a nine of availability buys you
workedExample.setup: Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by a factor of ten. A 30-day month has 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. Multiply that by the fraction of time the service may be down to get the allowed downtime.

conclusion.text: Going from two nines to four cuts a month's outages from most of a working day to about four minutes. Teams that need that guarantee move to dedicated deployments.

checkQuestion.prompt: A dedicated deployment promises four nines (99.99%) of availability. How many minutes of downtime does that allow in a 30-day month?
checkQuestion.methodHint: Count the minutes in the month, then multiply by the fraction of time the service may be down.
checkQuestion.explanation: Four nines leaves 0.01% of the month for outages: about four minutes. If you use 1% (two nines) by mistake, you get 432 minutes, a hundred times too many.
checkQuestion.sourceQuote: possible to achieve four nines or better with dedicated deployments of open models

reflect.prompt: Explain to a product manager why switching from a closed-model API to an open model you deploy yourself changes what your team can promise users. Name the three dimensions the Preface highlights.
reflect.modelAnswer: With a closed API we get whatever latency, uptime and price the vendor offers, tuned for all its customers at once. If we run an open model ourselves, those three become engineering decisions. We can tune the deployment for low latency on our own traffic, where the vendor tunes for throughput. We can run redundant dedicated capacity and aim for four nines. At our volume we can also pay far less per token, because we pick the hardware, the batching and the model size. In exchange, we own the serving work: deploying the model, scaling it and keeping it up.
points: Latency: you can tune a dedicated deployment for your users' real-time traffic.
Availability: dedicated deployments can reach four nines where an API offers two.
Cost: at scale, an open model can cost a fraction as much per token.
Control has a price: your team owns the serving work.
